events.title: Intel Pentium introduced
events.summary: Intel announced the Pentium processor on March 22, 1993 — the first x86 [CPU] marketed by brand name instead of model number.
events.about: The Pentium doubled performance over 486 chips with superscalar execution — Windows NT, Linux, and early 3D games demanded the extra headroom. The infamous FDIV bug made headlines, but Pentium became synonymous with [PC] CPUs through the 1990s. Developers optimizing for desktop performance targeted Pentium pipelines for years.

narrative.whyChosen: Pentium was Intel's defining consumer [CPU] brand of the 1990s [PC] boom.
narrative.whyImportant: It brought superscalar x86 performance to mainstream desktops and workstations.
narrative.problemSolved: 486-class CPUs could not keep pace with multimedia, GUIs, and server workloads of the early 1990s.

events.title: Lynx 2.0 gains World Wide Web support
events.summary: Lynx 2.0 shipped in March 1993 with World Wide Web support — turning the University of Kansas text browser into a terminal client for [HTML] pages.
events.about: Lynx rendered pages as plain text in a terminal: links listed by number, no images, no JavaScript. It stayed essential on slow connections, blind-accessible browsing, and server-side automation for decades — and still runs today for scripting and accessibility testing.

narrative.whyChosen: Lynx 2.0 brought the early web to text terminals before [Mosaic] popularized graphics.
narrative.whyImportant: It made the web usable on Unix shells and influenced accessibility and command-line tooling.
narrative.problemSolved: Researchers and students on Unix shells needed a keyboard-driven way to read [HTML] documents.
